terms.definition: The repeating cycle of context assembly → model call → decision → tool execution → result-fed-back that continues until the model returns end_turn or an exit condition is hit. See the Mental Model page for the full 8-step version.

One agent (the coordinator) delegates scoped subtasks to specialized subagents and explicitly threads their outputs back together. Subagents don't share memory automatically — the coordinator is the only thing that sees everything.
A coordinator evaluates a subagent's (or its own) output for gaps or errors and re-delegates a targeted follow-up before proceeding, instead of always moving forward linearly.
Sending simple queries around an expensive multi-agent pipeline (straight to a direct answer) instead of always paying the latency/cost of the full orchestration.
An explicit, designed hand-off to a human or a fallback flow when an agent can't resolve a task or hits a hard limit — the alternative to an agent looping indefinitely or guessing.
A hard ceiling on how many loop iterations an agent can take before being forced to stop and resolve or escalate, preventing an unbounded loop from running away.
The shape of how multiple agent calls relate: sequential (each depends on the last), parallel (independent, run concurrently), or hierarchical (coordinator/subagent).

Persisting each agent's structured output to a known location (not just conversation history) so a coordinator can reload a manifest and resume with only the relevant state after a failure, instead of replaying entire transcripts.

The deterministic code around the model that assembles context, calls the API, parses responses, executes tools, and enforces gates. Claude Code, an internal agent server, and a CI pipeline invoking Claude are all examples of a harness.
A field on the API response telling the harness why the model stopped generating — commonly end_turn (finished, no tool needed) or tool_use (requesting one or more tool calls).
An open protocol for connecting an LLM application to external tools/data sources through standardized servers, so a tool integration can be built once and reused across different agent harnesses.
A process that exposes a set of tools/resources via MCP. Configured at project scope (.mcp.json, shared with the team) or user scope (personal/experimental).
The structured definition (name, description, input parameters) that tells the model what a tool does and how to call it — this is what the model reasons over, not the backend implementation.
A tool parameter that returns a preview of an action's effect without actually performing it — required as an enforced gate for destructive or high-stakes tools, not just an optional nicety.

A transient error (timeout, 503) is safe to retry; a permanent/business error (validation failure, permission denied) never resolves by retrying. Tool error responses should be distinct types so retry logic can tell them apart.

How reliably a model picks the correct tool among the ones available. Degrades as the tool library grows — mitigated by discovery tools (e.g. a search_connectors-style tool) or scoping which tools are visible per context.
Writing tool descriptions so similarly-named or similarly-behaved tools (archive vs. delete) can't be confused under ambiguous phrasing.
A tool error that states what went wrong and what to try next, instead of a bare failure — lets the model self-correct on the next turn rather than repeating the same failing call.
Returning a tool's output as parseable JSON (specific fields) rather than free text, when a downstream caller needs to reliably extract those fields.

A prose memory/instruction file read automatically each session. Precedence: enterprise-managed policy > project CLAUDE.md > user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) > nested directory-level files. It's guidance the model reads, not enforced config.

A stored, reusable, versioned prompt/workflow (e.g. /migrate-component) shared across a team via the project repo — the mechanism for turning a workflow into something repeatable, but not something enforced.

Code that fires automatically on a lifecycle event (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SessionStart, etc.) — the mechanism for enforcement, unlike a slash command or CLAUDE.md instruction which the model could still deviate from.
A read-only exploration mode where Claude proposes a plan before any edit or command executes — reserved for changes with meaningful complexity or risk, not every trivial edit.

Controls how tool calls are gated: default (prompts for uncovered calls), acceptEdits (auto-accepts file edits only), plan (no execution at all), bypassPermissions (skips all prompts — trusted/sandboxed use only).
A custom agent (.claude/agents/*.md) with its own frontmatter and system prompt, scoped to a specific kind of task within a project.
Summarizing a long conversation to free up context space (/compact) while retaining key details — distinct from /clear, which wipes history entirely.

Running Claude Code without a human at the keyboard (e.g. in a CI pipeline). Tool permission scoping still fully applies — there being no live approver doesn't relax what the agent is allowed to touch.
Model output constrained to a defined schema (typically JSON) so downstream code can parse it reliably, instead of extracting fields from free text.

Feeding a schema/validation error back to the model and asking it to correct just that issue. Resolves most transient/format failures quickly, but can't fix systematic gaps (e.g. information the source document never contained).
Checking that structured output is correct in meaning (totals reconcile, an enum value reflects reality), not just that it parses — schema validation alone never catches this class of error.
An explicit "other" value in an enum field so a legitimate real-world value outside the sampled schema doesn't fail validation outright.
When information is genuinely absent from a source, correct behavior is returning null for that field — the failure mode to watch for is the model fabricating a plausible-but-invented value instead.
Large tool/schema definitions competing with a large input document for context space, which can degrade extraction accuracy well before the document actually hits the context window's hard limit.

Routing low-confidence model outputs to human review while auto-accepting high-confidence ones — valid only once you've confirmed with real data that high-confidence outputs are actually reliable at that threshold.

Delayed, discounted-cost processing suited to workloads with an hours-long SLA tolerance — requires planning a reprocessing path for items that fail individually (e.g. exceeding context length) within the batch.
The maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can process in a single request, including system prompt, conversation history, tool definitions, and tool results combined.

Long conversations lose recall of specific earlier details (names, numbers, stated preferences) well before the context window is technically full — a distinct failure from simply running out of space.

Dropping the oldest messages once a length limit is hit. Loses information outright rather than compressing it — persistent facts need to be extracted and carried forward separately, not left to survive truncation by luck.

Deliberately pulling out standing facts (identity, safety-critical details, ongoing preferences) so they survive truncation or session boundaries, instead of relying on them staying in the raw conversation history.

Adherence to system-prompt instructions weakens over long conversations (roughly 10-30+ turns) — countered by periodically re-anchoring the persona/instructions or summarizing and re-injecting core directives.
Large tool outputs (e.g. big JSON blobs from a lookup) consuming context faster than the conversation itself — mitigated by trimming or summarizing stale tool results once they're no longer needed.
Carrying key facts across separate sessions (days/weeks apart) requires deliberate persistence — a new conversation does not automatically inherit context from a prior one.
Feeding a mid-conversation external update (e.g. a webhook firing) into context so the assistant's next response reflects current reality without the user having to restate it.

Too many clarifying questions before acting causes task abandonment; too few causes acting on wrong assumptions. The right balance depends on the cost of guessing wrong for that specific task, not a fixed rule.

A hard, code-level check (spend limit, permission scope, allow/deny rule) applied before a requested tool call executes. Enforced in the harness — no prompt instruction can substitute for it, because the model's output is a request, not a guarantee.
The exam's core mental model: User/Entry Point, the Harness, the Model, the Claude API, and Tool Backends — see the Mental Model page for the full breakdown of each role.
